the middle value when the numbers are placed in order; half the values sit below it
a typical distance of the values from the mean; larger means more spread out
a bar graph where each bar counts how many values fall in a range
a shape whose left and right halves mirror each other
a shape with one tail stretched much farther out than the other

look.title: Two Classes, One Mean
look.text: Class A quiz scores: 7, 8, 8, 9. Class B quiz scores: 4, 6, 10, 12. Both totals are 32, so both means are 32 ÷ 4 = 8. For Class A the deviations are −1, 0, 0, 1; squares 1, 0, 0, 1; sum 2; 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5; standard deviation √0.5 ≈ 0.71. For Class B the deviations are −4, −2, 2, 4; squares 16, 4, 4, 16; sum 40; 40 ÷ 4 = 10; standard deviation √10 ≈ 3.16.
look.prompt: Both classes average 8. Which class would you rather be a random student in if you needed to score at least a 6, and how does the standard deviation tell you that?

check.q: The values 4, 8, 9 and 11 have what mean?
check.why: 4 + 8 + 9 + 11 = 32, and 32 ÷ 4 = 8. Choosing 8.5 comes from averaging the two middle values (the median), and 32 is the total, not the mean.

check.q: For the sleep data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (mean 5), what is the standard deviation when you divide the squared deviations by the count?
check.why: The squared deviations sum to 32; 32 ÷ 8 = 4; √4 = 2. Answering 4 forgets the square root, and 32 stops at the sum.

check.q: A histogram of home prices in a city has a long tail stretching to the right. Which statement is true?
choices: The mean and median are equal
The median is larger than the mean
The mean is larger than the median
check.why: A few very expensive homes pull the mean up, so in a right-skewed distribution the mean sits above the median.

lessons.title: The Normal Curve and the 68-95-99.7 Rule
lessons.mainIdea: When data follow a normal curve, about 68% fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2, and 99.7% within 3.
reading: Many measurements, such as heights of adults of the same sex, pile up in a smooth bell shape: highest at the mean, symmetric, tails thinning out on both sides. This bell is the *normal curve*, and it is completely described by two numbers, its mean and its standard deviation. Suppose a model for adult women's heights uses a mean of 64 inches and a standard deviation of 2.5 inches. The peak of the bell is at 64. One standard deviation on each side reaches from 64 − 2.5 = 61.5 to 64 + 2.5 = 66.5 inches.

The *empirical rule* says what fraction of a normal pile sits in those bands. About 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. For the height model: about 68% of women are between 61.5 and 66.5 inches; about 95% are between 64 − 5 = 59 and 64 + 5 = 69 inches; about 99.7% are between 56.5 and 71.5 inches. Because the curve is symmetric, each half of a band holds half its percent. So 34% are between 64 and 66.5, and 34% are between 61.5 and 64.

Now the ends. If 95% are within 2 standard deviations, the other 5% are outside, split evenly: 2.5% below 59 inches and 2.5% above 69 inches. If 68% are within 1 standard deviation, 32% are outside, so 16% are above 66.5 inches. A common error is to forget the split and say 32% are above 66.5. Another is to add standard deviations without multiplying: 2 standard deviations above 64 is 64 + 2 × 2.5 = 69, not 64 + 2 = 66. Write the band endpoints first, then read off the percents.

words.d: the symmetric bell-shaped curve, described entirely by its mean and standard deviation
for a normal curve, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean
the thin far ends of a distribution, where few values fall

look.title: How Much of the Bell Is in Each Band
rows: more than 2 SD above the mean
more than 3 SD above the mean
look.cite: standard normal distribution, standard table values rounded to one decimal
look.prompt: Using the 95% band, what percent of values are more than 2 standard deviations below the mean? Why does the table's 2.3 differ slightly from your answer?

check.q: Scores on a test are normal with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Between which two scores do about 95% of people fall?
check.why: Two standard deviations is 2 × 15 = 30, so the 95% band runs from 100 − 30 = 70 to 100 + 30 = 130. The 85-to-115 band holds only 68%.

check.q: With the same mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15, about what percent of people score above 115?
check.why: 115 is 1 standard deviation above the mean. 68% are within 1 SD, so 32% are outside, and half of those, 16%, are above.

check.q: Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, about what percent of values fall between the mean and 1 standard deviation above the mean?
check.why: 68% lie within 1 SD on both sides; by symmetry half of that, 34%, lies on the upper side between the mean and 1 SD above.

lessons.title: Z-Scores Measure Distance in Standard Deviations
lessons.mainIdea: A z-score tells how many standard deviations a value sits above or below the mean, so scores from different scales can be compared.
reading: A history test has mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Jada scores 82. How unusual is that? Measure her distance from the mean in units of standard deviation: 82 − 70 = 12 points above the mean, and 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 standard deviations. That number, 1.5, is her *z-score*. The formula is z = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation. A score of 58 gives z = (58 − 70) ÷ 8 = −12 ÷ 8 = −1.5, the same distance but below the mean. The sign matters: positive means above, negative means below.

Z-scores let you compare things measured on different scales. Suppose Test A has mean 500 and standard deviation 100, and Test B has mean 20 and standard deviation 5. Luis scores 650 on Test A and 28 on Test B. Which is the stronger result? On A: z = (650 − 500) ÷ 100 = 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5. On B: z = (28 − 20) ÷ 5 = 8 ÷ 5 = 1.6. The 28 is slightly farther above its mean, so it is the stronger performance, even though 650 is a much bigger number.

You can also go backwards. If a value has z = 2 on the 100-and-15 scale, it is 2 × 15 = 30 points above 100, so the value is 130. In general, value = mean + z × standard deviation. Two mistakes are common: dividing the raw value by the standard deviation without subtracting the mean first (82 ÷ 8 ≈ 10.25, which means nothing), and dropping the negative sign on values below the mean. Always subtract, then divide, and keep the sign.

words.d: how many standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean
convert a value into a z-score so it can be compared with values on other scales
the original measured value before it is turned into a z-score

look.title: Which Runner Had the Better Day?
look.text: In a girls' cross-country league, 5K times have mean 22.0 minutes and standard deviation 2.0 minutes. In the boys' league the mean is 19.0 minutes and the standard deviation is 1.5 minutes. Ana runs 19.0 minutes; Theo runs 16.6 minutes. For times, a faster run is a lower number, so a more negative z-score is better. Ana: z = (19.0 − 22.0) ÷ 2.0 = −1.5. Theo: z = (16.6 − 19.0) ÷ 1.5 = −1.6.
look.prompt: Who ran farther below their league's average, measured in standard deviations? Could the answer change if the boys' standard deviation were 2.0 instead of 1.5? Work it out.

check.q: A distribution has mean 50 and standard deviation 10. What is the z-score of the value 35?
check.why: z = (35 − 50) ÷ 10 = −15 ÷ 10 = −1.5. Dropping the sign gives 1.5; forgetting to divide gives −15.

check.q: On a scale with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, which raw score has a z-score of 2?
check.why: value = 100 + 2 × 15 = 130. Answering 115 uses only 1 standard deviation; 102 adds z without multiplying.

check.q: Test A: mean 80, SD 4, Priya scores 86. Test B: mean 60, SD 10, Priya scores 72. Which result is relatively stronger?
choices: Test B, because 72 is a bigger gain of 12 points
Test B, because its z-score is 1.5
Test A, because its z-score of 1.5 beats Test B's 1.2
check.why: Test A: (86 − 80) ÷ 4 = 1.5. Test B: (72 − 60) ÷ 10 = 1.2. The larger z-score, 1.5, is the stronger relative result even though the point gain is smaller.

sections.title: Percentiles and the Limits of the Model

lessons.title: From a Z-Score to a Percentile
lessons.mainIdea: A percentile is the percent of values below a given value; on a normal curve, the z-score tells you the percentile through a standard table.
reading: Back to Nia's height chart. A *percentile* is the percent of the group that falls below a value. On a normal curve, each z-score matches one percentile, and a short table gives the match. A value exactly at the mean has z = 0 and is the 50th percentile: half the group is below. A value with z = 1 is at about the 84th percentile, because 50% are below the mean and another 34% are between the mean and 1 standard deviation above, and 50 + 34 = 84. A value with z = −1 is at about the 16th percentile, since 50 − 34 = 16.

The table fills in the values between. The z-score for the 90th percentile is about 1.28. If six-year-old girls' heights are modeled with mean 45 inches and standard deviation 2 inches, then the 90th percentile height is 45 + 1.28 × 2 = 45 + 2.56 ≈ 47.6 inches. That is roughly where the nurse's dot for Nia fell. Going the other way, a score of 82 on the test with mean 70 and standard deviation 8 has z = 1.5, and the table gives about 93% below, so 82 is at the 93rd percentile.

To find the percent between two values, find each percentile and subtract. Between z = −1 (about 15.9%) and z = 0.5 (about 69.1%): 69.1 − 15.9 = 53.2% of values. Two cautions. First, a percentile is a rank, not an amount: the 90th percentile is not twice the 45th. Second, the table only works if the data are actually normal, which is the subject of the next lesson. A student who plugs a skewed data set into a z-table will get a tidy percent that is simply wrong.

words.d: the percent of the group whose values fall below a given value; the 90th percentile is above 90% of the group
a table that gives, for each z-score, the percent of a normal curve below it
a position in an ordered group, as opposed to an amount

look.title: Percent of a Normal Curve Below Each Z-Score
look.cite: standard normal table, rounded to one decimal
look.prompt: A student's z-score is 0.5 on one test and −0.5 on another. Use the table to find each percentile, then find the percent of the group that scored between those two z-scores.

check.q: On a normal curve, a value with z-score 1 is at about which percentile?
check.why: 50% lie below the mean and 34% lie between the mean and 1 SD above, so 50 + 34 = 84%. The 16th percentile belongs to z = −1.

check.q: A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Using the table (z = 1.5 gives about 93.3% below), at what percentile is a score of 82?
check.why: z = (82 − 70) ÷ 8 = 1.5, and the table gives about 93% of scores below, so 82 is at the 93rd percentile.

check.q: Using the table, about what percent of values lie between z = −1 (15.9% below) and z = 0.5 (69.1% below)?
check.why: Subtract the lower percentile from the upper: 69.1 − 15.9 = 53.2%. Adding them (85%) counts the wrong region.

lessons.title: When the Normal Model Fits
lessons.mainIdea: Use the normal model only when the data are roughly symmetric and bell-shaped; skewed, two-peaked or bounded data break it.
reading: The normal curve is a model, and a model can be wrong. Before using z-scores or the empirical rule, look at a histogram. Heights of adult men, measurement errors, and averages of many small effects tend to be close to normal. Household income is not: most households are near the middle, but a few earn enormous amounts, and the tail on the right stretches for miles. Time waiting in line is not either: it cannot go below zero, but it can run very long. A normal model applied to either would predict percents that never happen.

Here is a quick test. Suppose a data set of wait times has mean 10 minutes and standard deviation 8 minutes. If the data were normal, the empirical rule would put 2.5% of waits below 10 − 2 × 8 = −6 minutes. A negative wait is impossible, so the model cannot fit. Any time the mean is less than about two standard deviations from a hard boundary such as zero, the normal curve is a poor choice. A second test is to count: if far fewer than 68% of the values are within 1 standard deviation of the mean, the shape is not a bell.

*Bimodal* data, which have two separate peaks, also break the model. Ages at a middle-school open house are bimodal: one hump near 13 for students and one near 42 for parents. The mean, somewhere around 28, describes almost nobody, and a z-score built from it is meaningless. When the model does not fit, use percentiles computed directly from the sorted data instead of from a z-table, and report the median and the middle 50% rather than the mean and standard deviation.

words.d: a simplified mathematical description of real data that may fit well or badly
a distribution with two distinct peaks, often from two different groups mixed together
a hard limit that values cannot cross, such as zero for a wait time
having a long tail of large values on the right, so the mean exceeds the median

look.title: Three Data Sets, One Question
look.text: Set 1: the number of siblings for 200 students; most have 0, 1 or 2, a few have 6 or more, and none can have fewer than 0. Set 2: the heights of 200 adult women, with mean 64 inches, standard deviation 2.5 inches, and 137 of the 200 within 61.5 to 66.5 inches. Set 3: the ages of 200 people at a school open house, with a peak near 13 and another near 42.
look.prompt: For each set, decide whether a normal model fits and name the specific feature (boundary, skew, two peaks, or a good 68% check) that decided it. Note that 137 ÷ 200 = 68.5%.

check.q: Which data set is most likely to be well described by a normal curve?
choices: Heights of adult men in Illinois
Number of cars owned per household
Ages of everyone at a middle-school open house
check.why: Adult heights pile up symmetrically around the mean. Incomes are right-skewed, car counts are bounded at zero and skewed, and open-house ages are bimodal.

check.q: A data set of delivery times has mean 20 minutes and standard deviation 15 minutes. Why does the normal model fit poorly?
choices: The standard deviation is too small
The model would put about 2.5% of deliveries below −10 minutes, which is impossible
The model would put 95% of deliveries above 50 minutes
check.why: Two standard deviations below the mean is 20 − 30 = −10 minutes. A normal model expects 2.5% of values there, but a negative time cannot occur.

check.q: A histogram shows two clear peaks. What is the best description?
choices: Normal with a large standard deviation
Bimodal, likely two groups mixed together
check.why: Two peaks mean the data are bimodal, usually because two different groups were combined; a single normal curve has only one peak.

lessons.title: Independence and the Multiplication Rule
lessons.mainIdea: When two events are independent, the probability that both happen is the product of their separate probabilities.
reading: Flip a coin twice. The chance of heads on the first flip is 1/2, and the coin has no memory, so the chance of heads on the second flip is still 1/2 no matter what happened first. Two events are *independent* when one happening does not change the probability of the other. For independent events, the *multiplication rule* gives the chance that both happen: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). So P(heads, then heads) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. You can check by listing the four equally likely outcomes, HH, HT, TH, TT: exactly one of the four is HH.

A basketball player makes 80% of her free throws. If her shots are independent, the chance she makes two in a row is 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64. The chance she misses at least one of the two is everything else: 1 − 0.64 = 0.36. That subtraction uses the *complement*: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The chance of three makes in a row is 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512, so even a good shooter misses at least one of three shots almost half the time.

Drawing without replacement is the classic case where independence fails. Pull one card from a standard 52-card deck: P(ace) = 4/52. Keep it out and pull a second: if the first was an ace, only 3 aces remain among 51 cards, so P(second ace) = 3/51. The chance of two aces is 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221. A common mistake is to multiply 4/52 × 4/52 as if the deck had been reset; that overstates the chance. Before multiplying, ask whether the first event changes the odds for the second.

words.d: two events are independent when one happening does not change the probability of the other
for independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B)
the event that A does not happen; P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
drawing items and not putting them back, so later draws have changed probabilities

look.title: Two Alarms
look.text: Devon sets two independent alarms to wake up for the train. Each alarm goes off on time with probability 0.9. The chance both alarms fail is 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01, so the chance at least one alarm works is 1 − 0.01 = 0.99. If the two alarms were on the same phone and that phone's battery dies 10% of the time, the failures would not be independent: one dead battery kills both alarms.
look.prompt: With three independent alarms each at 0.9, what is the chance at least one works? Then explain why two alarms on one phone might be no better than one.

check.q: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability of rolling a 6 both times?
check.why: The rolls are independent, so P = 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. Adding the probabilities (2/6) is the mistake of using the wrong rule.

check.q: Three independent parts each work with probability 0.9. What is the probability all three work?
check.why: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.729. Adding gives 2.7, which is impossible for a probability; 0.271 is the chance at least one fails.

check.q: Which pair of events is NOT independent?
choices: Two flips of a fair coin
Rolling a die today and rolling it tomorrow
Drawing two cards from a deck without replacement
Two spins of a fair spinner
check.why: Once a card is removed, the makeup of the deck changes, so the second draw's probabilities depend on the first. The other pairs have no such link.

lessons.title: Conditional Probability and Two-Way Tables
lessons.mainIdea: A conditional probability restricts attention to one row or column of a table; if it matches the overall probability, the events are independent.
reading: A survey of 200 students asks two yes-or-no questions: do you play a school sport, and do you have a part-time job? The results fit in a *two-way table*. Of the 120 who play a sport, 40 have a job and 80 do not. Of the 80 who do not play a sport, 30 have a job and 50 do not. Column totals: 70 have a job, 130 do not. The overall chance that a randomly chosen student has a job is 70/200 = 0.35.

A *conditional probability* asks about a smaller group. Given that a student plays a sport, what is the chance they have a job? Now only the 120 sport players matter, and 40 of them have jobs: P(job | sport) = 40/120 = 1/3 ≈ 0.333. The vertical bar reads 'given.' Flip the condition: P(sport | job) = 40/70 = 4/7 ≈ 0.571, because now the 70 job holders are the whole world and 40 of them play a sport. Notice these two are different numbers; mixing them up is the most common error in this topic.

Conditional probability gives a clean test for independence: two events are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A). Here P(job | sport) ≈ 0.333 but P(job) = 0.35, and P(job | not sport) = 30/80 = 0.375. The numbers are close but not equal, so job and sport are slightly linked: sport players are a little less likely to hold a job. When a table has raw counts, always divide by the total of the row or column you are conditioning on, never by the grand total.

words.d: a table that counts how many items fall into each combination of two categories
the probability of A given that B is known to have happened, written P(A | B)
the word that signals a condition: 'the chance of rain given that it is cloudy'
the total count of everything in a two-way table

look.title: Cracked Screens
look.text: A repair shop logs 100 phones. Among the 60 phones that had a case, 10 had a cracked screen and 50 did not. Among the 40 phones without a case, 20 had a cracked screen and 20 did not. So 30 of the 100 phones were cracked overall. P(cracked | case) = 10/60 = 1/6 ≈ 0.17. P(cracked | no case) = 20/40 = 1/2 = 0.5.
look.prompt: Find P(cracked) for all 100 phones and compare it to the two conditional probabilities. Are having a case and cracking the screen independent? What does the comparison suggest, and what does it not prove?

check.q: In the student survey (120 play a sport, 40 of them have a job), what is P(job | sport)?
check.why: Condition on the 120 sport players; 40 of them have a job, so 40/120 = 1/3. Dividing by 200 uses the grand total, and 40/70 is P(sport | job).

check.q: Same survey: 70 students have a job and 40 of those play a sport. What is P(sport | job)?
check.why: Condition on the 70 job holders: 40/70 = 4/7 ≈ 0.57. The answer 1/3 is the reversed condition P(job | sport).

check.q: Two events A and B are independent exactly when which statement is true?
choices: P(A | B) is larger than P(A)
check.why: Independence means knowing B does not change the chance of A, so the conditional probability equals the plain probability.

lessons.title: The Addition Rule
lessons.mainIdea: To find the chance that A or B happens, add their probabilities and subtract the overlap so nothing is counted twice.
reading: Draw one card from a standard deck. What is the chance it is an ace or a heart? There are 4 aces and 13 hearts, but the ace of hearts is in both groups. Adding 4 + 13 = 17 counts that card twice. The *addition rule* fixes this: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). So P(ace or heart) = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Check by counting: 4 aces plus the 12 hearts that are not aces gives 16 favorable cards out of 52.

Some events cannot happen together. Rolling a 1 and rolling a 2 on the same die are *mutually exclusive*: the overlap is empty and P(A and B) = 0. Then the rule simplifies to P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. Now try 'even or greater than 4.' Even is {2, 4, 6}, probability 3/6. Greater than 4 is {5, 6}, probability 2/6. Both at once is {6}, probability 1/6. So P = 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. Listing the winning faces, {2, 4, 5, 6}, confirms 4 out of 6.

Two mistakes come up again and again. The first is adding probabilities for events that overlap without subtracting: a student says P(even or greater than 4) = 5/6, which counts the 6 twice. The second is confusing 'or' with 'and': 'and' asks for both, which is the overlap and is found by multiplying (when independent) or by reading the table cell, never by adding. Word the question to yourself first: is it 'both,' or is it 'at least one'?

words.d: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B); subtract the overlap so it is not counted twice
two events that cannot both happen at once, so their overlap has probability 0
the outcomes that belong to both events, written A and B

look.title: Coffee or Tea
look.text: At a school fundraiser, 50% of adults order coffee, 30% order tea, and 10% order both. The chance an adult orders coffee or tea is 0.5 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.7, so 30% order neither. Check with a picture: two overlapping circles, with 0.1 in the overlap, 0.4 in coffee only, 0.2 in tea only, and 0.3 outside both, adding to 1.0.
look.prompt: Suppose instead that nobody orders both. What would P(coffee or tea) be, and what would the picture look like? Then explain why P(coffee or tea) can never be larger than 0.8 in the original setup.

check.q: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.3 and P(A and B) = 0.1. What is P(A or B)?
check.why: 0.5 + 0.3 − 0.1 = 0.7. Answering 0.8 forgets to subtract the overlap; 0.15 multiplies instead of adding.

check.q: One roll of a fair die: what is the probability of an even number or a number greater than 4?
check.why: P(even) = 3/6, P(greater than 4) = 2/6, overlap {6} = 1/6, so 3/6 + 2/6 − 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. The winning faces are 2, 4, 5 and 6.

check.q: What does it mean for two events to be mutually exclusive?
choices: They cannot both happen on the same trial
check.why: Mutually exclusive events have no shared outcomes, so P(A and B) = 0 and the addition rule needs no subtraction.

lessons.title: Expected Value and Decisions
lessons.mainIdea: Expected value is the long-run average result per trial: multiply each outcome by its probability and add.
reading: A club sells 100 raffle tickets at $2 each, and one ticket wins a $100 prize. If you buy one ticket, what do you get back on average? You win $100 with probability 1/100 and $0 with probability 99/100. The *expected value* of the prize is 100 × 1/100 + 0 × 99/100 = $1. You paid $2, so your expected net result is 1 − 2 = −$1 per ticket. That does not mean you lose exactly $1; you lose $2 or gain $98. It means that over many tickets your average result is a loss of $1 each, which is exactly how the club makes money.

The general recipe: list every outcome, multiply each by its probability, and add the products. A game pays the number of dollars showing on one roll of a fair die. The expected payout is 1 × 1/6 + 2 × 1/6 + 3 × 1/6 + 4 × 1/6 + 5 × 1/6 + 6 × 1/6 = 21/6 = $3.50. A fair price to play would be $3.50; at $4 the house wins 50 cents per game on average. A common error is to average the outcomes without their probabilities, which only works when all outcomes are equally likely, as they happen to be here.

Expected value guides decisions, but it is not the only consideration. A phone-repair plan costs $60 a year. Suppose a phone breaks with probability 0.1 in a year and the repair costs $300. Expected repair cost without the plan: 0.1 × 300 + 0.9 × 0 = $30. The plan costs $60, twice the expected loss, so on average it is a bad deal. But a person who could not possibly pay $300 at once might reasonably buy it anyway: expected value tells you the average, not how much a bad outcome would hurt. Report the expected value, then talk about the risk.

words.d: the long-run average result per trial, found by adding each outcome times its probability
a game whose expected net result is zero for the player
how far the actual outcomes can swing from the expected value, and how much a bad swing would hurt
what you gain or lose after subtracting what you paid

look.title: Payouts on One Spin of a Prize Wheel
look.cite: example wheel defined for this lesson; probabilities sum to 1
look.prompt: Compute the expected payout: 0 × 0.6 + 1 × 0.25 + 5 × 0.1 + 20 × 0.05. If a spin costs $2, what is the expected net result, and who comes out ahead over 1,000 spins?

check.q: A spinner pays $10 with probability 0.2 and costs you $2 with probability 0.8. What is the expected net result per spin?
check.why: 10 × 0.2 = 2 gained, 2 × 0.8 = 1.6 lost, and 2 − 1.6 = 0.40. Forgetting the loss side gives $2; forgetting the win side gives −$1.60.

check.q: A raffle sells 1,000 tickets at $5 each and gives one $2,000 prize. What is the expected net result of buying one ticket?
check.why: Expected prize is 2,000 × 1/1,000 = $2. Subtract the $5 cost: 2 − 5 = −$3 per ticket on average.

check.q: Option A pays a sure $50. Option B pays $120 with probability 0.5 and $0 otherwise. Which statement is correct?
choices: A has the higher expected value, $50 versus $40
B has the higher expected value, but it is also riskier
B has the higher expected value and no extra risk
check.why: B's expected value is 120 × 0.5 = $60, more than A's $50, but B can pay nothing half the time while A never does.

lessons.title: The Binomial Setting
lessons.mainIdea: When you repeat the same independent yes-or-no trial a fixed number of times, the count of successes follows a binomial distribution.
reading: A free-throw shooter who makes half her shots takes 4 shots. How likely is exactly 2 makes? This is a *binomial setting*: a fixed number of trials (4), each with two outcomes (make or miss), the same probability of success on each (0.5), and independent trials. Write all 16 equally likely sequences of M and X. Exactly 2 makes happens in 6 of them: MMXX, MXMX, MXXM, XMMX, XMXM, XXMM. So P(exactly 2) = 6/16 = 0.375.

Counting sequences by hand gets slow, so use the pattern. The number of ways to choose which k of the n trials are successes is written C(n, k). For n = 4: C(4, 0) = 1, C(4, 1) = 4, C(4, 2) = 6, C(4, 3) = 4, C(4, 4) = 1. Each specific sequence with k successes has probability p^k × (1 − p)^(n − k). Multiply: P(k successes) = C(n, k) × p^k × (1 − p)^(n − k). For an 80% shooter taking 3 shots, P(exactly 2 makes) = C(3, 2) × 0.8^2 × 0.2^1 = 3 × 0.64 × 0.2 = 0.384.

Check the whole distribution for that shooter: P(0) = 1 × 0.2^3 = 0.008; P(1) = 3 × 0.8 × 0.04 = 0.096; P(2) = 0.384; P(3) = 0.8^3 = 0.512. The four add to 1.000, which is a good sign that nothing was dropped. Two things break the binomial setting: a probability that changes from trial to trial (drawing cards without replacement), and a number of trials that is not fixed in advance (shooting until the first miss). Check the four conditions before using the formula.

words.d: a fixed number of independent trials, each a success or failure with the same probability
one repetition of the chance process, such as one shot or one flip
the outcome being counted, whatever it is; a 'success' can even be a defect
the number of ways to choose which k of n trials are successes; C(4, 2) = 6

look.title: Four Fair Coin Flips: Chance of Each Number of Heads
look.cite: binomial distribution with n = 4 and p = 0.5; counts 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 out of 16
look.prompt: Why is the table symmetric? What would change about the shape if the coin landed heads 80% of the time? Compute the new chance of 4 heads.

check.q: A fair coin is flipped 3 times. What is the probability of exactly 1 head?
check.why: Three sequences have exactly one head (HTT, THT, TTH) out of 8 equally likely sequences, so 3/8. Answering 1/8 counts only one sequence.

check.q: A player makes 80% of free throws. In 3 independent shots, what is the probability of exactly 2 makes?
check.why: C(3, 2) × 0.8^2 × 0.2 = 3 × 0.64 × 0.2 = 0.384. Forgetting the 3 ways gives 0.128; 0.512 is all three makes.

check.q: Which situation is a binomial setting?
choices: Counting the number of sixes in 10 rolls of a fair die
Drawing cards without replacement until you find an ace
Rolling a die until the first six appears
check.why: Ten fixed independent rolls, each a six or not with probability 1/6, meets all four conditions. The others have changing probabilities, a non-fixed number of trials, or no yes-or-no outcome.

lessons.title: Mean and Spread of a Binomial Count
lessons.mainIdea: In a binomial setting the expected count is n × p and the standard deviation is √(n × p × (1 − p)), which tells you which counts are unusual.
reading: If a 70% free-throw shooter takes 100 shots, how many makes should we expect? Common sense says about 70, and the formula agrees: the *mean* of a binomial count is n × p = 100 × 0.7 = 70. The count varies from night to night, and its *standard deviation* is √(n × p × (1 − p)) = √(100 × 0.7 × 0.3) = √21 ≈ 4.6 makes. For a large n the binomial pile is close to a normal curve, so the empirical rule applies: on about 95% of 100-shot nights she makes between 70 − 2 × 4.6 ≈ 61 and 70 + 2 × 4.6 ≈ 79.

That spread lets you judge a claim. A student guesses randomly on a 20-question multiple-choice test with 4 choices each, so p = 0.25. Mean = 20 × 0.25 = 5 correct. Standard deviation = √(20 × 0.25 × 0.75) = √3.75 ≈ 1.94. Suppose the student gets 12 right. The z-score is (12 − 5) ÷ 1.94 ≈ 3.6, far beyond 3 standard deviations. Pure guessing almost never produces that, so the honest conclusion is that the student knew something (or copied). The formula turned a hunch into a number.

Flip a coin 100 times and get 65 heads. Is the coin fair? For a fair coin, mean = 50 and standard deviation = √(100 × 0.5 × 0.5) = √25 = 5. Then 65 heads is (65 − 50) ÷ 5 = 3 standard deviations above the mean, a result the empirical rule puts at about 1 in 1,000 for the upper tail alone. That is strong evidence against fairness, and it is the first step toward the hypothesis tests of the next chapter. A common slip is to take √(n × p) and forget the (1 − p) factor: √50 ≈ 7.1 would wrongly make 65 heads look ordinary.

words.d: the expected number of successes, n × p
the spread of the success count, √(n × p × (1 − p))
a result more than about 2 standard deviations from what the model expects

look.title: The Unlucky Sixes
look.text: Rowan rolls a die 180 times and gets only 18 sixes. Expected sixes: 180 × 1/6 = 30. Standard deviation: √(180 × 1/6 × 5/6) = √25 = 5. The z-score for 18 is (18 − 30) ÷ 5 = −2.4, more than 2 standard deviations below the mean. Under a fair die this happens on fewer than 1 in 100 tries.
look.prompt: Is 18 sixes unusual enough to suspect the die? Now suppose Rowan had rolled 24 sixes instead. Find that z-score and decide whether it would raise your suspicion.

check.q: A fair coin is flipped 400 times. What are the mean and standard deviation of the number of heads?
check.why: Mean = 400 × 0.5 = 200. SD = √(400 × 0.5 × 0.5) = √100 = 10. Forgetting the square root gives 100; using √(n × p) gives √200 ≈ 14.1.

check.q: A process succeeds 20% of the time. In 50 independent tries, what is the expected number of successes?
check.why: n × p = 50 × 0.2 = 10. Answering 20 confuses the percent with the count.

check.q: A coin flipped 100 times gives 65 heads. Using mean 50 and standard deviation 5, what is the z-score, and what does it suggest?
choices: z = 3, strong evidence the coin is not fair
check.why: (65 − 50) ÷ 5 = 3. A result 3 standard deviations above the mean is expected on only about 1 in 1,000 fair-coin tries.

review.q: For the values 3, 5, 5, 7 (mean 5), what is the standard deviation when you divide by the count?
review.why: Deviations −2, 0, 0, 2; squares 4, 0, 0, 4 sum to 8; 8 ÷ 4 = 2; √2 ≈ 1.41. Stopping at 2 forgets the square root.

review.q: Heights are modeled as normal with mean 64 inches and standard deviation 2.5 inches. About what percent are taller than 69 inches?
review.why: 69 is 2 standard deviations above 64. About 5% lie outside the 95% band, and half of those, 2.5%, are above.

review.q: Which z-score corresponds to a raw score of 58 when the mean is 70 and the standard deviation is 8?
review.why: (58 − 70) ÷ 8 = −12 ÷ 8 = −1.5. Keeping the sign matters; −12 forgets to divide.

review.q: A test score is at the 84th percentile of a normal distribution. About what is its z-score?
review.why: The 84th percentile matches z = 1, since 50% are below the mean and 34% more lie within 1 SD above it.

review.q: A two-way table shows 60 phones with a case, 10 of them cracked, and 40 without a case, 20 of them cracked. What is P(cracked | no case)?
review.why: Condition on the 40 phones without a case: 20/40 = 1/2. The overall rate 30/100 = 3/10 uses the wrong total.

review.q: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and A and B are independent. What is P(A or B)?
review.why: Independent, so P(A and B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2. Then 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.7. Answering 0.9 forgets to subtract the overlap.

review.q: A game pays $6 with probability 1/3 and $0 otherwise, and costs $3 to play. What is the expected net result?
review.why: Expected payout is 6 × 1/3 = $2. Subtract the $3 cost: 2 − 3 = −$1 per game.

review.q: A shooter makes 60% of free throws and takes 100 independent shots. What is the standard deviation of the number of makes?
review.why: √(100 × 0.6 × 0.4) = √24 ≈ 4.9. Answering 24 forgets the square root; √60 ≈ 7.7 drops the (1 − p) factor.

chapters.title: Sampling, Inference and Claims
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a few hundred people tell us about millions, and when should we refuse to believe what a number claims?

story.title: Two Million Ballots and the Wrong Answer
story.kicker: In 1936 a famous magazine collected more than two million responses and still predicted the wrong president. The problem was not the count.
paragraphs: In the fall of 1936 the Literary Digest, a popular American magazine, ran the biggest straw poll anyone had ever attempted. It mailed roughly ten million postcard ballots asking who the reader would vote for: President Franklin Roosevelt or the Republican challenger, Alf Landon. More than two million cards came back. The magazine had called the previous several elections correctly with the same method, and it announced its forecast with confidence: Landon would win comfortably, with a clear majority of the vote.

Roosevelt won in a landslide, carrying all but two states and roughly 61% of the popular vote. The magazine had missed by nearly 20 percentage points with a sample a thousand times larger than most polls use today. What went wrong? The Digest had built its mailing list from telephone directories, automobile registrations and its own subscribers. In the middle of the Great Depression, people who owned a phone or a car were, on average, wealthier than people who did not, and wealthier voters leaned toward Landon. The list itself was tilted before a single card was mailed.

There was a second problem. Only about one card in four came back. People who bother to return a mail-in ballot are not a random slice of the people who received one; they tend to be angrier, more engaged, or more eager for change. That year, the voters most motivated to respond were the ones who wanted Roosevelt out. Two tilts, one in who was asked and one in who answered, pointed the same way, and no amount of extra postcards could fix them. A bigger biased sample is just a bigger mistake.

Meanwhile a young researcher named George Gallup predicted Roosevelt's win using a sample of only tens of thousands of people, chosen to look like the whole electorate. His question was not 'how many people can we ask?' but 'who are we asking, and who are we missing?' That question is the heart of this chapter. You will learn how a small random sample can stand in for a huge population, how much it can be trusted, how to test a claim against data, and how to read a headline built on numbers without being fooled.
story.think: Suppose the Literary Digest had mailed twenty million cards instead of ten million, using the same lists. Would its prediction have gotten better, worse, or stayed about the same? Explain.

sections.title: Collecting Data That Can Be Trusted

lessons.title: Populations, Samples and Statistics
lessons.mainIdea: A population is the whole group you want to know about; a sample is the part you actually measure, and a statistic from it estimates a parameter of the population.
reading: Chicago Public Schools serves more than 300,000 students. A student newspaper wants to know what fraction of them ride a CTA bus or train to school. Asking every student is a *census*, which is slow and expensive. Instead the paper asks 500 students. The whole group of interest, every CPS student, is the *population*. The 500 who are asked are the *sample*. If 310 of the 500 say yes, the sample proportion is 310 ÷ 500 = 0.62, or 62%.

That 62% is a *statistic*: a number computed from the sample. The true fraction of all CPS students who ride the CTA, whatever it is, is a *parameter*: a fixed number about the population that we usually never learn exactly. Statistics estimate parameters. A second sample of 500 might give 295 ÷ 500 = 0.59. Neither is wrong; each is an estimate, and the rest of the chapter is about how close such estimates tend to be. Keep the vocabulary straight: parameter goes with population, statistic goes with sample.

The same words apply to averages. If the mean commute time in the sample of 500 is 34 minutes, that sample mean is a statistic estimating the parameter, the mean commute of all 300,000 students. Two common confusions: calling the sample the population (the 500 students are not 'everyone'), and treating the statistic as if it were exact (writing 'exactly 62% of CPS students ride the CTA'). A careful sentence says 'about 62% of the students surveyed,' and then asks how far off that might be.

words.d: the entire group you want to draw conclusions about
the part of the population you actually measure
an attempt to measure every member of the population, like the U.S. Census every ten years
a number that describes the whole population, usually unknown
a number computed from a sample, used to estimate a parameter

look.title: Counting Everyone: 2020 Census Populations
look.cite: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 Census counts, rounded
look.prompt: The Census tries to count everyone rather than sample. About what fraction of Illinois residents live in Chicago? If a pollster wanted a sample that looks like Illinois, why would sampling only in Chicago be a problem?

check.q: A newspaper surveys 500 of the more than 300,000 CPS students. Which is the population?
check.why: The population is the whole group the paper wants to describe, all CPS students. The 500 are the sample.

check.q: In the survey, 310 of 500 students ride the CTA. The value 62% is best called what?
check.why: 62% is computed from the sample, so it is a statistic. The true percent for all students is the parameter it estimates.

check.q: Why do two random samples of 500 from the same population usually give slightly different percentages?
choices: One of the samples must have been done wrong
Different samples contain different people, so estimates vary
Percentages cannot be computed from samples
check.why: Sampling variability is normal: each random sample is a different set of people, so the statistic moves a little even when the parameter does not.

lessons.title: Surveys, Observational Studies and Experiments
lessons.mainIdea: A survey asks, an observational study watches, and an experiment assigns treatments; only an experiment can show that one thing causes another.
reading: Three ways to collect data answer three different kinds of question. A *survey* asks people to report something: who they will vote for, how many hours they sleep, whether they ride the CTA. An *observational study* records what people already do and looks for patterns, such as comparing the grades of students who eat breakfast with the grades of those who skip it. An *experiment* actively assigns a *treatment*: the researcher decides which students get breakfast and which do not, then compares.

The difference matters because of *confounding*. Suppose the observational study finds that breakfast eaters average 8 points higher. Did breakfast cause the gain? Maybe. But students who eat breakfast may also sleep more, have more organized mornings, or come from homes with more support, and any of those could be the real reason. A hidden variable tangled up with the one you are studying is a confounder, and observation alone cannot untangle it. The study shows an association, not a cause.

An experiment breaks the tangle by random assignment. Flip a coin for each of 200 volunteers: heads eats a provided breakfast for a month, tails does not. Chance, not personal habits, decides who is in which group, so sleep, family support and everything else are spread roughly evenly across both groups. If the breakfast group then scores higher, breakfast is the most reasonable explanation. Whenever you read that something 'causes' or 'leads to' an outcome, ask: did the researchers assign it, or just observe it?

words.d: a study that collects data by asking people questions
a study that records what happens without controlling who gets what
a study in which the researcher assigns treatments to subjects, ideally at random
the condition given to a group in an experiment, such as a new drug or a new lesson plan
when a hidden variable is mixed up with the one being studied, so you cannot tell which caused the result

look.title: Ice Cream and Drownings
look.text: In many cities, months with higher ice cream sales also have more drownings. Nobody assigned ice cream to anyone; this is an observation. The confounder is summer heat: hot weather sends people both to the ice cream stand and to the pool or lake. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together without one causing the other.
look.prompt: Describe an observational finding you have heard reported as a cause (for example, about screen time, coffee or a diet). Name a possible confounder, then sketch an experiment that could actually test the claim.

check.q: Researchers compare test scores of students who chose to attend tutoring with scores of students who did not. What type of study is this?
check.why: The students chose for themselves; the researchers only observed and compared. Nothing was assigned, so it is observational.

check.q: What is the main advantage of randomly assigning subjects to treatment groups?
choices: It spreads hidden differences evenly across groups, so the treatment is the likely cause of any difference
It removes the need for a control group
check.why: Random assignment balances confounders such as habits or background between groups, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment.

check.q: A study finds that people who own more books have higher incomes. Which is the most careful conclusion?
choices: Owning books and income are associated, but a confounder such as education could explain both
The study proves nothing at all
check.why: An observational link is an association. Education plausibly drives both book ownership and income, and the study cannot rule it out, but the association is still real information.

lessons.title: Random Samples and Sources of Bias
lessons.mainIdea: A simple random sample gives every group of the same size the same chance of being chosen; anything that tilts who is asked or who answers is bias.
reading: A *simple random sample* is chosen so that every possible group of the chosen size has the same chance of being picked. To draw 60 students at random from a school of 1,200, number the students 1 to 1,200, and let a random number generator pick 60 different numbers. No student can lobby to be included or excluded, and no teacher's opinion of who is 'typical' enters in. That is the point: chance does the choosing, so the sample's tilt, if any, is only the luck of the draw, which the next lessons show how to measure.

*Bias* is a systematic tilt, a reason the sample tends to differ from the population in a predictable direction. The Literary Digest showed two kinds. *Undercoverage* means parts of the population never had a chance to be picked: no phone, no car, no subscription meant no ballot. *Nonresponse* bias arises when the people who answer differ from those who do not. A third kind, *voluntary response*, is worse still: a website poll that anyone can click answers only the question 'who felt strongly enough to click?' A survey of sports fans who volunteer to rate the team's coach will not describe the average fan.

Convenience samples, such as asking the first 50 people at the cafeteria door, share the same flaw: the people at the door at 11:15 are not a random slice of the school. Wording matters too. 'Do you support the plan to cut wasteful spending?' and 'Do you support the plan to cut school programs?' can describe the same plan and get opposite answers. When you judge a sample, ask three questions: who was left out, who did not answer, and what exactly was asked?

words.d: a sample chosen by chance so every group of the same size is equally likely to be picked
a systematic tilt that makes a sample differ from the population in a predictable direction
when part of the population has no chance of being selected
when the people who refuse or fail to answer differ from those who do
a sample made of people who chose to participate, usually those with strong opinions

look.title: Four Ways to Ask the School
look.text: A student council wants to know what fraction of the 1,200 students want a later start time. Plan A: post a poll on social media and count the votes. Plan B: ask the 40 students in the council's own homerooms. Plan C: number all students and pick 100 with a random number generator, then follow up with anyone who does not reply. Plan D: stand at the parking lot exit and ask 100 drivers.
look.prompt: Name the type of bias in Plans A, B and D. Why is the follow-up step in Plan C important, and what would go wrong without it?

check.q: A TV station asks viewers to text in whether they support a new stadium, and 78% say yes. What is the main problem?
choices: Voluntary response: only people who felt strongly bothered to text
Texting is not a valid way to collect data
The station should have used a census
check.why: People who choose to respond are not a random slice of the viewers, let alone the city. The 78% describes the texters, not the public.

check.q: A poll of Illinois voters is drawn only from people with landline phones. What kind of bias is this?
check.why: Voters without a landline never had a chance to be selected, which is undercoverage. Nonresponse concerns people who were selected but did not answer.

check.q: Which method produces a simple random sample of 60 from a school of 1,200 students?
choices: Number every student and let a random number generator pick 60 distinct numbers
Take the first 60 students who arrive on Monday
Ask each teacher to nominate 3 typical students
Choose 60 students from the honors classes
check.why: Only the numbered random draw gives every group of 60 the same chance. Arrival time, teacher choice and class type all create bias.

lessons.title: Why Samples Differ From Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: Even perfect random samples give different results each time; the pattern of those results, the sampling distribution, is predictable.
reading: Imagine a jar of 10,000 beads, exactly half red and half white, so the true proportion of red is p = 0.5. Scoop out 100 beads at random and count the red ones. You might get 47. Put them back, stir, scoop again: 53. Again: 49, 55, 44. None of these is wrong. This bead-to-bead wobble is *sampling variability*, and it happens even when the sampling is done perfectly. The parameter never moved; only the sample did.

Now imagine doing 1,000 scoops of 100 and making a histogram of the 1,000 sample proportions. That histogram is the *sampling distribution*. For random samples it has a beautiful regularity: it is centered at the true value 0.5, it is roughly bell-shaped, and its spread depends on the sample size. Most scoops of 100 fall between 0.40 and 0.60. If instead each scoop held 400 beads, the histogram would be much narrower, with most scoops between 0.45 and 0.55.

Two lessons follow. First, a single sample's proportion is a draw from this distribution, so it is 'off' by a typical amount you can estimate. Second, bigger samples shrink that typical amount, but only for random samples. If the jar were stirred badly so that red beads sat on top, every scoop would run red, and scooping 400 instead of 100 would not help. Sampling variability is chance and can be reduced by size; bias is a tilt and cannot.

words.d: the natural chance difference between one random sample's result and the next
the pattern of values a statistic takes over many repeated random samples
the number of individuals in the sample, written n

look.title: Ten Random Scoops of 100 Beads From a Half-Red Jar
look.cite: example results generated for this lesson from a jar with exactly 50% red beads
look.prompt: What is the mean of the eight counts? How far is the farthest scoop from 50? If the jar were 60% red, roughly where would you expect the scoops to cluster?

check.q: A jar is exactly half red. A random scoop of 100 beads has 44 red. What is the best explanation?
choices: The jar is not really half red
Sampling variability: random samples naturally vary around the true value
Counting 44 is impossible for a fair scoop
check.why: Even from a perfectly mixed jar, scoops of 100 typically range from about 40 to 60 red. A 44 is ordinary chance variation.

check.q: Which change makes the sampling distribution of a sample proportion narrower?
choices: Asking a more strongly worded question
Sampling only from people who volunteer
check.why: Larger random samples vary less from sample to sample. Wording and volunteering add bias, which is a tilt, not a change in spread.

check.q: A sampling distribution built from many random samples of the same size is centered where?
check.why: Random samples scatter evenly around the parameter, so the center of the sampling distribution is the population value itself.

lessons.title: Simulating a Sampling Distribution
lessons.mainIdea: Simulate many random samples with coins, dice or a computer to see how far a statistic typically strays; the spread shrinks like 1 divided by the square root of n.
reading: You do not need a jar of beads. To *simulate* sampling 100 people from a population where half say yes, flip a coin 100 times and count heads. Each run of 100 flips is one simulated sample. Do it 50 times and you have a rough sampling distribution. A computer can do 10,000 runs in a second, but the idea is the same: rebuild the chance process, run it many times, and look at what the results usually do.

The simulated histogram has a spread you can predict with the binomial formula from the last chapter. For a proportion, the *standard error* is √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n). With p = 0.5 and n = 100: √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100) = √0.0025 = 0.05. So about 95% of simulated sample proportions land within 2 × 0.05 = 0.10 of 0.5, that is, between 0.40 and 0.60, matching the bead scoops. With n = 400: √(0.25 ÷ 400) = √0.000625 = 0.025, so 95% land between 0.45 and 0.55.

Notice the pattern: quadrupling n from 100 to 400 cut the spread in half, from 0.05 to 0.025. The spread shrinks with the square root of n, not with n itself. To cut it in half again you would need 1,600, and to reach a spread of 0.01 you would need 2,500. Doubling the sample only makes it about 1.4 times more precise. That is why polls of about 1,000 people are so common: they give a standard error near 0.016, a margin of about 3 points, and going to 10,000 people costs ten times as much just to bring the margin down to about 1 point.

words.d: imitate a chance process many times with coins, dice, cards or a computer to see its typical results
the standard deviation of a statistic across repeated samples; for a proportion it is √(p(1 − p) ÷ n)
the spread of a sample statistic shrinks in proportion to 1 ÷ √n, so four times the sample halves the spread

look.title: Is 62 Heads in 100 Flips Surprising?
look.text: A student flips a coin 100 times and gets 62 heads, a proportion of 0.62. For a fair coin the standard error is √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100) = 0.05, so 0.62 is (0.62 − 0.50) ÷ 0.05 = 2.4 standard errors above 0.5. In a simulation of 10,000 fair-coin runs of 100 flips, only about 1 run in 100 gives 62 or more heads.
look.prompt: If the student had flipped 400 times and gotten 62% heads, what would the standard error and the number of standard errors be? Which result is stronger evidence that the coin is unfair, and why?

check.q: For a population proportion of 0.5, what is the standard error of a sample proportion when n = 100?
check.why: √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 100) = √0.0025 = 0.05. Answering 0.0025 forgets the square root; 0.25 is p × (1 − p) without dividing.

check.q: A sample proportion has standard error 0.05 with n = 100. To make the standard error 0.025, what sample size is needed?
check.why: Halving the spread requires four times the sample, since spread shrinks with √n: √(0.25 ÷ 400) = 0.025.

check.q: In a simulation of 100 fair-coin flips repeated many times, about what range holds 95% of the sample proportions of heads?
check.why: The standard error is 0.05, and about 95% of results fall within 2 standard errors of 0.5: 0.5 ± 0.10 gives 0.40 to 0.60.

lessons.title: Margin of Error and Confidence Intervals
lessons.mainIdea: A confidence interval reports a sample estimate plus and minus a margin of error, a range that captures the true value in about 95% of samples.
reading: A poll of 1,000 Illinois adults finds 54% in favor of a new transit plan. The true percent for all adults is unknown, but the sampling distribution tells us how far a sample of 1,000 typically strays. Standard error: √(0.54 × 0.46 ÷ 1,000) = √0.0002484 ≈ 0.0158. Two standard errors is about 0.032, or 3.2 percentage points. That is the *margin of error*. The *confidence interval* is 54% ± 3.2%, from 50.8% to 57.2%. A pollster would write: '54%, with a margin of error of about 3 points.'

What does '95% confidence' mean? Not that there is a 95% chance the truth is in this one interval; the truth is a fixed number and is either in it or not. It means the method works 95% of the time: if you took many samples of 1,000 and built an interval from each, about 95 of every 100 intervals would capture the true value and about 5 would miss. You do not know whether yours is one of the 5, which is why a result at 50.8% to 57.2% supports 'more than half' only cautiously.

A quick rule for a 95% margin of error when p is near 0.5 is 1 ÷ √n. For n = 1,000: 1 ÷ √1,000 ≈ 1 ÷ 31.6 ≈ 0.032, matching the careful calculation. For n = 400 it is 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05, or 5 points; for n = 2,500 it is 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02, or 2 points. Two cautions: the margin of error covers only random sampling variability, not bias, and a poll with 60% ± 5% does not mean '60% is right and the rest is error.' Every value from 55% to 65% is consistent with the data.

words.d: the plus-or-minus amount around a sample estimate, about 2 standard errors for 95% confidence
the range from estimate minus margin of error to estimate plus margin of error
the method produces an interval that captures the true value in about 95 out of 100 samples
the difference between two percents; from 54% to 57% is 3 percentage points

look.title: Quick Margin of Error, 1 ÷ √n, for a Proportion Near 50%
look.prompt: Going from 100 to 400 people cuts the margin from 10 to 5. How many more people does it take to go from 5 to 2.5? From 2.5 to 1? What does that suggest about the cost of extra precision?

check.q: A random sample of 400 people finds 60% support a proposal. Using the 1 ÷ √n rule, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval?
check.why: 1 ÷ √400 = 1 ÷ 20 = 0.05, so the margin is 5 points and the interval is 60% ± 5%, or 55% to 65%.

check.q: A pollster wants to cut a margin of error from 4 points to 2 points. Roughly how must the sample size change?
check.why: Margin shrinks with √n, so halving the margin requires 4 times as many people. Doubling n only cuts the margin by a factor of about 1.4.

check.q: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is 50.8% to 57.2%. Which interpretation is correct?
choices: There is a 95% chance the sample proportion is in this range
95% of the population falls between 50.8% and 57.2%
The true value is definitely between 50.8% and 57.2%
This method captures the true value in about 95% of samples, and this interval is one such attempt
check.why: Confidence describes how often the method succeeds over many samples. The sample proportion is known exactly (54%), and the true value may or may not be inside.

lessons.title: The Logic of a Hypothesis Test
lessons.mainIdea: A hypothesis test assumes the claim is true, asks how surprising the data would then be, and rejects the claim only if the data are very unlikely under it.
reading: A friend hands you a coin and says it is fair. You flip it 100 times and get 60 heads. Fair coins usually give around 50, but 60 is not impossible. How do you decide? A *hypothesis test* works like a courtroom. The claim on trial, called the *null hypothesis*, is 'the coin is fair, p = 0.5.' It gets the benefit of the doubt. The *alternative hypothesis* is what you would conclude if the evidence is strong enough: 'the coin favors heads.' The data are the evidence, and the question is whether they are consistent with the null.

Assume the null is true and measure how unusual the result is. For a fair coin in 100 flips, the expected count is 50 with standard deviation √(100 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 5. Then 60 heads is (60 − 50) ÷ 5 = 2 standard deviations above expected. From the normal table, a fair coin produces 60 or more heads only about 2.3% of the time. That is rare. If we would see this in fewer than 5 of 100 tries, the usual convention says the result is *statistically significant*, and we reject the null: the evidence points to a coin that favors heads.

The logic has two sides that students often flip. Rejecting the null does not prove the alternative; it says the data would be surprising if the null were true, so the null is doubtful. And failing to reject does not prove the null; 54 heads is consistent with a fair coin, but also with a coin that has p = 0.52. A test can be wrong in two ways: rejecting a true null (convicting an innocent coin, which happens about 5% of the time at the 5% cutoff), or failing to reject a false null (letting a guilty coin go). Small samples make the second error common.

words.d: a procedure that judges a claim by asking how unlikely the observed data would be if the claim were true
the claim being tested, usually 'no effect' or 'no difference,' which gets the benefit of the doubt
the conclusion you adopt if the data make the null hypothesis hard to believe
so unlikely under the null hypothesis (usually under 5%) that the null is rejected

look.title: The Cafeteria's Claim
look.text: The cafeteria manager claims 80% of students like the new menu. A random sample of 50 students finds 32 who like it, a proportion of 0.64. Null hypothesis: p = 0.80. Under the null, the standard error is √(0.8 × 0.2 ÷ 50) = √0.0032 ≈ 0.057. The sample sits (0.64 − 0.80) ÷ 0.057 ≈ −2.8 standard errors below the claim. A result that far below happens well under 1% of the time if the claim is true.
look.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses in words. Should the manager's claim be rejected? What would you conclude if the sample had found 38 of 50 instead (proportion 0.76)?

check.q: A company claims its battery lasts 10 hours on average. In a test of the claim, what is the null hypothesis?
choices: The battery lasts less than 10 hours
The battery lasts more than 10 hours
The average battery life is 10 hours
check.why: The null hypothesis is the claim under test, stated as no difference from what is asserted: mean = 10 hours.

check.q: A fair coin flipped 100 times gives 60 heads, which is 2 standard deviations above 50. About how often does a fair coin do at least this well?
check.why: The upper tail beyond 2 standard deviations on a normal curve holds about 2.3%. Answering 16% uses the 1-SD tail.

check.q: A test fails to reject the null hypothesis that a coin is fair. What can you conclude?
choices: The data are consistent with a fair coin, but the null is not proven
The sample must have been too large
check.why: Failing to reject means the data were not surprising under the null. That is compatibility, not proof; a slightly unfair coin could give the same data.

lessons.title: How Surprising Is Surprising? The P-Value
lessons.mainIdea: The p-value is the chance of a result at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true; a small p-value is evidence against the null.
reading: The number that measures surprise is the *p-value*: the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed. For the coin with 60 heads in 100 flips, the p-value is about 0.023, the fair-coin chance of 60 or more heads. A p-value is not the chance the null is true; it is the chance of data like yours if the null is true. Those are different sentences, and swapping them is the most common misreading of statistics in news stories.

You can find a p-value by *simulation* instead of a table. Take the cafeteria claim that 80% of students like the menu, with a sample of 50 that found only 32. Program a computer to draw 50 'students' at random from a population where 80% say yes, count the yeses, and repeat 10,000 times. Then count how many of the 10,000 runs gave 32 or fewer. If about 60 runs did, the p-value is roughly 60 ÷ 10,000 = 0.006. The claim would produce a sample this low only about 6 times in 1,000, so we reject it.

The usual cutoff, called the *significance level*, is 0.05: reject the null when p is below it. But the cutoff is a convention, not a law of nature. A p-value of 0.06 is barely different from 0.04, and a p-value of 0.30 means the data are ordinary under the null, not that the null is true. Try one: a candidate claims 50% support, a random sample of 200 shows 55%. Standard error √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 200) ≈ 0.0354, so 0.55 is about 1.41 standard errors above 0.5, and the upper-tail p-value is about 0.08. Above 0.05, so not significant, even though 55 sounds like more than 50.

words.d: the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed
the cutoff, usually 0.05, below which a p-value leads to rejecting the null hypothesis
generating many fake samples from the null hypothesis to see how often results like yours occur
farther from what the null hypothesis expects than the observed result

look.title: Simulated Samples of 50 From a Population That Is 80% Yes
look.cite: binomial distribution with n = 50 and p = 0.8, grouped and rounded
look.prompt: The real sample found 32 yeses. Which row contains it, and what does that row's percent tell you about the p-value? Would a sample of 41 yeses give reason to doubt the 80% claim?

check.q: Which sentence correctly describes a p-value of 0.02?
choices: There is a 2% chance the null hypothesis is true
If the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 2% of the time
check.why: A p-value is a probability about the data given the null, not about the null itself. The first choice is the classic misreading.

check.q: A candidate claims 50% support. A random sample of 200 shows 55%, about 1.41 standard errors above 0.5, with p-value about 0.08. At the 0.05 level, what is the conclusion?
choices: Reject the claim; 55% is more than 50%
Do not reject the claim; a sample this high is not unusual if support is really 50%
The sample must have been biased
check.why: The p-value 0.08 is above 0.05, so the data are within ordinary sampling variability for p = 0.5. Sounding higher is not the same as being significantly higher.

check.q: In 10,000 simulated samples under the null hypothesis, 30 gave a result as extreme as the real one. What is the estimated p-value?
check.why: 30 ÷ 10,000 = 0.003. Answering 0.03 misplaces the decimal; 30 is a count, not a probability.

lessons.title: Statistical Versus Practical Significance
lessons.mainIdea: With a huge sample, even a tiny, unimportant difference becomes statistically significant; always ask how big the effect is, not just whether p is small.
reading: A tutoring company tests a new app on 50,000 students, split at random into two groups. The app group averages 70.5 on a final exam and the control group averages 70.0. Because the samples are enormous, the standard error of the difference is tiny, about 0.2 points, so a 0.5-point gap is 2.5 standard errors and the p-value is below 0.05. The result is statistically significant. It is also nearly worthless: half a point on a 100-point exam changes nobody's grade. The gap is real, but it is not important.

That is the difference between *statistical significance* and *practical significance*. Statistical significance answers: could this gap be a fluke of sampling? With 50,000 students, almost no gap is a fluke. Practical significance answers: is the gap big enough to matter to a student, a doctor or a city? Only judgment, not a formula, answers that. A report should always give the *effect size*, the actual difference or ratio, alongside the p-value, so a reader can see whether 0.5 points is worth an app subscription.

The mirror-image mistake happens with small samples. Suppose a new reading program is tried on 12 students and their scores rise 8 points on average, but with only 12 students the standard error is about 5 points, so the gain is 1.6 standard errors and the p-value is about 0.11, not significant. That does not mean the program failed; it means 12 students cannot tell an 8-point gain from noise. An honest summary says 'promising, but the study was too small to be sure.' Sample size decides what a study can detect; it does not decide what matters.

words.d: a result unlikely to be due to sampling variability alone, usually meaning p is below 0.05
an effect large enough to matter in real life, judged by its size, not by its p-value
the actual size of a difference or relationship, such as 0.5 points or a 2% drop in risk
a study's ability to detect a real effect; larger samples give more power

look.title: Two Headlines, Same Study
look.text: A city tests a new traffic light timing at 200 intersections for a year. Average wait per car drops from 42.0 seconds to 41.6 seconds, and with millions of cars measured the p-value is below 0.001. Headline A: 'New timing significantly cuts wait times.' Headline B: 'New timing saves drivers 0.4 seconds per light.' Both are accurate.
look.prompt: Which headline would you want as a driver, and which would you want as the company selling the system? Write one sentence that reports the finding fairly, with both the p-value and the effect size.

check.q: A study of 50,000 students finds a 0.5-point exam gain with a p-value below 0.05. What is the best description?
choices: Statistically significant but of little practical importance
Practically important but not statistically significant
Proof that the app should be adopted by every school
check.why: The huge sample makes even a half-point gap unlikely to be chance, but half a point on a 100-point test barely matters to anyone.

check.q: Why can a very large sample make a tiny difference statistically significant?
choices: Large samples are always biased toward finding effects
The standard error shrinks with sample size, so even small gaps become many standard errors wide
Large samples change the size of the effect
P-values are only defined for large samples
check.why: Standard error shrinks like 1 ÷ √n. With n huge, a 0.5-point gap divided by a 0.2-point standard error is 2.5 standard errors and significant.

check.q: A program tested on 12 students shows an 8-point gain with p = 0.11. What is the fairest conclusion?
choices: The program definitely works, since 8 points is large
The gain is promising, but the study was too small to separate it from chance
The p-value must be a mistake
check.why: A small sample has little power. Not significant means the data cannot rule out chance, not that the effect is zero; a larger study is the next step.

lessons.title: Headlines Built on Numbers
lessons.mainIdea: Before believing a data claim, ask who was sampled, how big the sample was, whether the effect is relative or absolute, and who paid for the study.
reading: 'Daily coffee linked to 20% lower risk!' Before sharing that, read it like a statistician. First, linked to is observational language: coffee drinkers may differ in exercise, income or sleep, so this is an association until an experiment says otherwise. Second, 20% lower than what? If the risk falls from 5 in 1,000 to 4 in 1,000, that is a 20% *relative* drop but only 1 in 1,000 in *absolute* terms. Relative percents make small changes sound enormous. Ask for the two actual rates every time.

Third, look for the sample. 'Nine out of ten dentists' means little without knowing how many dentists were asked, how they were chosen, and who asked them. A survey of 20 dentists selected by a toothpaste company is not the same as a random sample of 2,000. Also look for the margin of error. If a poll says a candidate leads 48% to 46% with a margin of error of 3 points, the intervals overlap, and the honest headline is 'too close to call,' not 'candidate takes the lead.' A 2-point gap inside a 3-point margin is noise.

Fourth, ask who benefits. A study funded by the company whose product it praises is not automatically wrong, but it deserves a closer look, and so does a result that has never been repeated by anyone else. Finally, watch the axes on any graph: a bar chart whose vertical axis starts at 90 instead of 0 can make a 2% difference look like a cliff. None of these checks requires a formula. They require the habit of asking 'compared to what, measured how, and says who?'

words.d: a change expressed as a percent of the starting value; 5 to 4 per 1,000 is a 20% relative drop
the plain difference between two rates; 5 to 4 per 1,000 is a drop of 1 per 1,000
two things tending to occur together, which does not by itself show one causes the other
repeating a study with new data to see whether the result holds up

look.title: Doubles Your Risk
look.text: A headline says a food additive doubles the risk of a rare illness. The study reports the rate rose from 2 in 100,000 to 4 in 100,000 among heavy users. Relative change: 4 ÷ 2 = 2, so the risk did double. Absolute change: 4 − 2 = 2 extra cases per 100,000 people, or 0.002 percentage points. The study was observational, and heavy users of the additive also ate more processed food overall.
look.prompt: Rewrite the headline so a reader sees both the relative and absolute change. Then name a confounder and say what kind of study would be needed to show cause.

check.q: A risk falls from 8 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000. What are the relative and absolute changes?
check.why: Absolute: 8 − 6 = 2 per 1,000. Relative: 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25, a 25% drop. Answering 75% confuses the remaining fraction with the drop.

check.q: A poll shows candidate A at 48% and candidate B at 46% with a margin of error of 3 points. Which headline is most accurate?
choices: The race is too close to call
check.why: Both estimates carry a ±3-point margin, so their intervals overlap. A 2-point gap is smaller than the sampling uncertainty.

check.q: A bar chart shows sales of 96 and 98 units, but the vertical axis starts at 95 so the second bar looks twice as tall. What is the problem?
choices: A truncated axis exaggerates a small difference of about 2%
Bar charts should never be used for sales
The chart needs a larger sample
check.why: Starting the axis at 95 makes a 2-unit gap (about 2%) look like a doubling. The numbers are fine; the picture misleads.

lessons.title: Experiments That Earn a Cause
lessons.mainIdea: Random assignment, a control group, blinding and replication are what let an experiment say 'this caused that.'
reading: To show that a treatment causes an outcome, an experiment needs four ingredients. First, a *control group* that does not get the treatment, so there is something to compare against. Second, *random assignment* of subjects to treatment or control, so the groups are alike except for the treatment. Third, when people's expectations could affect the result, a *placebo*, a fake treatment that looks real, and *blinding*, so subjects (and ideally the people measuring them) do not know who got which. Fourth, enough subjects that a real effect is not lost in sampling variability.

The 1954 field trial of the Salk polio vaccine is the classic example. Hundreds of thousands of American children were randomly assigned to receive the vaccine or a placebo injection, and neither the children nor the doctors diagnosing polio knew which was which. Polio cases were much rarer in the vaccinated group, and because assignment was random and diagnosis was blind, that difference could not be explained by which families volunteered or by doctors expecting vaccinated children to be healthier. The vaccine was declared effective and released to the public.

Compare a weaker design: give the vaccine to children whose parents ask for it and compare them with everyone else. Parents who ask for a vaccine tend to differ in income, education and health habits, so any difference in polio rates would be tangled with those. The lesson for reading any claim of cause: find the control group, find the word random, and ask whether anyone could have known who got what. When an experiment is impossible or unethical, as with smoking, researchers rely on many observational studies that point the same way, plus a plausible mechanism, and they say so.

words.d: the subjects who do not receive the treatment, used for comparison
using chance to decide which subjects get which treatment, balancing hidden differences
a fake treatment that looks like the real one, used so expectations affect both groups equally
keeping subjects, and often researchers, from knowing who received which treatment

look.title: Design the Sleep Study
look.text: A school wants to know whether a later 8:30 start time improves grades. Design 1: switch the whole school to 8:30 and compare this year's grades with last year's. Design 2: randomly assign half of the homerooms to a study hall that lets them arrive at 8:30, keep the other half at 7:30, and compare grades at the end of the semester. In Design 1, anything else that changed this year, new teachers, a new curriculum, a milder flu season, is a confounder.
look.prompt: Which design could support a cause claim, and why? Name one practical problem with running Design 2 and one thing you would measure besides grades.

check.q: What is the purpose of a placebo in a medical experiment?
choices: To increase the effect of the real treatment
So that expectations of being treated affect both groups equally
check.why: People who believe they are treated often feel better. A placebo gives the control group the same belief, so any extra improvement is due to the real treatment.

check.q: In the 1954 polio vaccine trial, why was random assignment essential?
choices: It made the groups alike in everything but the vaccine, so the lower polio rate could be credited to the vaccine
It guaranteed that no vaccinated child got polio
It let the doctors choose which children needed the vaccine most
It reduced the cost of the study
check.why: Random assignment spreads family income, health habits and other hidden factors evenly, so the only systematic difference between groups was the vaccine.

check.q: A company gives its new app to employees who volunteer and compares their productivity with everyone else's. What is the flaw?
choices: Volunteers likely differ from non-volunteers, so the groups are not comparable
The company should have used a placebo app on everyone
check.why: Self-selection means the app group may be more motivated to begin with. Without random assignment, that motivation, not the app, could explain the difference.

review.why: It is computed from the sample of 800, so it is a statistic that estimates the parameter, the mean commute of all residents.

review.q: The 1936 Literary Digest poll used lists of phone and car owners. Which type of bias does this illustrate?
review.why: Voters without phones or cars had no chance to be selected, so a whole part of the population was left out of the sampling frame.

review.q: For a proportion near 0.5, the standard error with n = 400 is 0.025. What is it with n = 1,600?
review.why: Four times the sample halves the standard error: 0.025 ÷ 2 = 0.0125. Check: √(0.25 ÷ 1,600) = √0.00015625 = 0.0125.

review.q: A random sample of 2,500 voters gives 52% for a measure. Using 1 ÷ √n, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval?
A coin flipped 100 times shows 58 heads. With mean 50 and standard deviation 5, what is the z-score, and is it significant at the 5% level (one-sided cutoff about 1.65)?
review.why: (58 − 50) ÷ 5 = 1.6, which falls just short of the one-sided 5% cutoff of about 1.65, so the result is not significant. Forgetting to divide gives 8.

review.q: Which statement about a p-value of 0.40 is correct?
choices: The null hypothesis is 40% likely to be true
Data like these are common if the null hypothesis is true, so there is little evidence against it
The sample must be enlarged by 40%
review.why: A large p-value means the observed result is ordinary under the null; it neither proves nor strongly challenges the null.

review.q: A study of 1,000,000 shoppers finds that a new checkout layout saves an average of 1.2 seconds per visit, p below 0.001. Which is the best description?
choices: Statistically significant, and the effect size decides whether it matters in practice
Proof that the layout should be copied everywhere
review.why: With a million shoppers, a tiny gap is easily significant. Whether 1.2 seconds is worth the cost of the change is a question of effect size and judgment.

review.q: Which study design could justify the claim 'the new fertilizer causes taller corn'?
choices: Randomly assign plots to fertilizer or no fertilizer and compare heights
Compare farms that chose the fertilizer with farms that did not
Survey farmers about whether they think it works
Measure corn height on one farm before and after using it
review.why: Only random assignment with a control group balances soil, weather and farmer skill across groups, so height differences can be credited to the fertilizer.
